headline: Futures bounce and oil slips about 2% before the open, helped by Trump's waiver of new Russia oil tariffs and a China GDP beat, but the money behind AI data centers is still cracking and French bonds are selling off.
summary: Dashboard prices are still Friday Oct 16 closes (refreshed Oct 17); today's moves below are premarket. S&P 500 futures were up 0.47% and Nasdaq futures about 0.7% to 1.2% early Monday, the 10 year yield eased to about 5.085%, and Brent fell about 2% to $107.60 from Friday's $109.86 settle. The oil drop comes from Trump's Oct 16 waiver of the Graham Act's tariffs on Russian oil buyers, not from Hormuz, which is still shut. China grew 4.5% in Q3, a touch above the 4.4% forecast, but shoppers stayed weak; Korea bounced 1.8% while Tokyo and Taipei slipped. Microsoft walked away from a UK AI site that had no power, and Oracle linked data center loans trade below par. No put idea passes today, and PFE is still the only swing setup.

regime.why: A green premarket after the worst Nasdaq week since June is a bounce, not a turn: the chip index just matched its longest losing streak since 2008, and lenders are still pulling back from AI borrowers. Oil and yields easing help, and Tuesday through Thursday earnings will decide the week. Normal size only on breakouts that close over the pivot on 1.5x volume; do not chase the open.

signals.title: Oil slips about 2% before the open because Trump waived the Graham Act's Russia oil tariffs, not because Hormuz opened
signals.since_yesterday: Brent fell 2.06% to $107.60 by 2am ET Monday. The driver is the Oct 16 waiver of new Russia tariffs and sanctions, which earlier briefs missed; Hormuz is still shut.
signals.what_happened: On Oct 16, two days before they took effect, Trump signed a national interest waiver of the Graham Act's Russia measures: tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods, tariffs of up to 100% on the top five buyers of Russian crude and gas, and the bank sanctions (CNBC, ABC). Sanctions from earlier executive orders stay, and the waiver can be reversed. Bloomberg reported the goal is to get more Russian diesel onto world markets before the Nov 3 midterms. Brent fell 2.06% to $107.60 and WTI 1.6% to $99.80 at 2am ET Monday, against Friday settles of $109.86 and $101.41 (ADVFN); Reuters had Brent near $107 later in the morning. Hormuz is still closed to normal traffic. Iran's seven day reopening plan has no US answer, and Iranian state media claimed another tanker caught fire after a mine strike; no maritime authority has confirmed it.
signals.so_what: Who gets paid: India and China, the biggest buyers of Russian crude, no longer face a 100% US tariff, and diesel users (truckers, airlines) get a little relief. Who pays: US producers lose some of the war premium, and Ukraine loses leverage. Oil is still near $107, far above prewar levels, so this trims the premium rather than removing it. What would make it wrong: a new Hormuz strike, or Ukraine knocking out more Russian refineries, which would cut diesel exports anyway.
signals.for_you: Swing: if you hold energy swings, keep the dashboard stops. XOM (178.98), CVX (224.99), COP (146.51) and EOG (158.01) were in uptrends with up/down volume 1.2 to 1.45 on Friday, so a 2% oil dip is not a sell signal by itself; just do not add on a red open. Airlines: UAL (96.10) is rated Avoid and reports Tuesday; DAL (75.37) is rated Wait. No puts on either. Long term: no action.

signals.title: AI names bounce premarket, but the money behind data centers keeps cracking: Microsoft walks away from a UK site with no power, and Oracle linked loans trade below par
signals.what_happened: Nasdaq 100 futures rose about 0.7% to 1.2% early Monday, with Nvidia up 1.1%, Broadcom 2.3% and CoreWeave 1.3% premarket; Intel rose 3.8% after JPMorgan upgraded it to neutral (Reuters, Oct 19). That follows a chip index slide of eight sessions, matching its longest since October 2008 (Reuters; Stocktwits put the loss near $2 trillion). Over the weekend the Telegraph reported, and Reuters and Bloomberg confirmed on Oct 18, that Microsoft ended its deal for Nscale's Loughton, Essex site, billed as the UK's largest AI data center, where it was to rent about 23,000 Nvidia chips. Grid officials did not expect power there until the 2030s. Nscale says the relationship is still strong, but the news hits its planned US IPO. Debt for Oracle's Michigan campus has fallen to about 87 cents on the dollar from par in July, and Oracle's 5 year default swaps are near a record 300 basis points (EnterpriseAM, Oct 19; Motley Fool, Oct 16). A newsletter said 80 cents; that figure could not be confirmed. Where power exists, deals still close: on Oct 16 NiSource signed a 20 year, 1,100 MW supply deal for Microsoft's Indiana campus starting in 2028, with Microsoft paying for the generation (NiSource).
signals.so_what: Power, not chips, now decides which AI sites get built. Customers walk from sites without grid power and pay for sites with it, which favors owners of firm power and grid equipment over borrowed money neoclouds. Second order: Nvidia demand is not in question at the hyperscalers, but chip rental demand at small lenders' customers is. Third order: banks holding unsold data center loans will lend less to the next project. One green premarket does not end an eight day slide; Meta's capex guide on Wednesday is the real test.
signals.for_you: Swing: no chip swings on a gap up. NVDA (214.13) is 'Buy zone, wait for the chart'; wait for a close over a pivot on 1.5x volume. Long term: MSFT (529.05) is 'Buy zone now' but near the top of its zone; small tranche only. ORCL (128.23) is rated Wait, below its 140.30 to 163.80 zone and in a downtrend. A director bought about $3.48 million near $139.35 on Sep 29 (filed Oct 1, 18 days old), so he is about 8% under water; it is one buyer, not a cluster. Puts: none on ORCL or CRWV while lenders set their prices.

signals.title: World check: China beats at 4.5% but shoppers stay weak, Korea bounces while Tokyo and Taipei slip, Brazil's race tightens, and French bonds sell off
signals.since_yesterday: China's Q3 GDP came in at 4.5% against 4.4% expected, and a new AtlasIntel poll cut Flavio Bolsonaro's lead to 2.2 points.
signals.what_happened: China: GDP grew 4.5% from a year ago and 1.2% from Q2, versus 4.4% and 1.0% expected; growth for the first nine months is 4.6%, inside the 4.5% to 5% target (Xinhua, FXStreet). September factory output rose 5.5%, but retail sales rose only about 1.1% (not in every report) and fixed asset investment fell 7.2% for January to September. The statistics bureau said weak domestic demand 'remains prominent' (Eastern Herald). Asia Monday (AP): the KOSPI rose 1.8% to 5,768.01 but is still down more than 17% in a month; the Nikkei fell 0.6% to 64,916.70; the Taiex fell 0.6% to 46,822 with TSMC flat at NT$2,420 (Focus Taiwan). Hong Kong was closed for a holiday (Newsquawk). A Shanghai close was not found. Brazil: AtlasIntel has Flavio Bolsonaro at 49.8% to Lula's 47.6% (51.1% to 48.9% of valid votes), down from a 5.4 point lead on Oct 9; Nexus for BTG has 46.5% to 45.9% (Rio Times, Reuters). France: after a weekend of riots, the 10 year yield rose to about 4.84% to 4.89%, the gap over German bonds reached about 142 to 146 basis points, and the CAC 40 fell about 1% to 1.4% by midday, with Societe Generale and BNP Paribas down more than 2% (CNBC, Bloomberg). Parliament votes on budget revenues Oct 20 and Moody's reviews France Oct 23.
signals.so_what: China's beat came from factories and exports, not shoppers, and analysts say it gives Beijing less reason for big stimulus in Q4. That is a mild negative for copper and China consumer stocks. Korea's bounce follows the worst week for Samsung and SK hynix since 2008; foreigners sold about $7.8 billion of Korean stocks last week (Seoul Economic Daily), so treat it as a bounce. Brazil: polls are tightening while betting markets still give Bolsonaro about 77% to 80%, so a Lula upset is the risk the market has not priced. France: rising yields and falling banks are a fiscal stress signal; a Moody's downgrade Friday would add to it.
signals.for_you: No action. FCX (69.54, 'Accumulate on pullback') and SCCO (200.51, 'Buy zone, wait for the chart'): less stimulus removes one support, so do not buy early. NU (14.56) is 'Buy zone now', but wait until after the Oct 25 vote to buy or sell puts. Korean bank ADRs (KB 118.81, SHG 70.31) stay hurt into Thursday's rate decision. No dashboard name is French. NU, ITUB and EWZ are left out of both lists because the vote is still a coin flip.

signals.title: Earnings: Cleveland-Cliffs and Fifth Third beat this morning; RTX, GE, GM, 3M, United, Netflix and Intuitive Surgical all report Tuesday, not today
signals.what_happened: Cleveland-Cliffs posted adjusted EPS of $0.28 against $0.21 expected on revenue of $5.6 billion, a bit under the $5.7 billion forecast (Newsquawk). Adjusted EBITDA was $612 million, up from $286 million in Q2 and above its $575 million guide, on 4.2 million tons shipped; it plans a large debt paydown in Q4 (company release). Fifth Third reported EPS of $0.90, or $1.13 adjusted, against about $1.09 expected, in its first full quarter with Comerica (SEC 8-K, Zacks). After today's close: Steel Dynamics, Zions, Western Alliance, W. R. Berkley, AGNC and Crown Holdings (Kiplinger, XTB). Checked: none of RTX, GE Aerospace, GM, 3M, United Airlines, Netflix or Intuitive Surgical report today; all are Tuesday Oct 20. RTX reports before the open; Intuitive's call is 1:30pm Pacific (4:30pm ET). Analysts expect Intuitive EPS of about $2.61 to $2.65 on revenue near $2.88 billion (Zacks, TipRanks).
signals.so_what: Cliffs is the only US maker of the electrical steel that goes into transformers, so a strong quarter fits the grid shortage story; its debt is the reason the dashboard still rates it Avoid. Tonight's regional banks (Zions, Western Alliance) are the read on credit after last week's private credit stress. Tuesday is the big day for her lists: RTX tests the defense rally, United tests jet fuel costs, and Intuitive tests whether surgical robot growth can hold at a premium price.
signals.for_you: Swing: no new swings in names that report this week. Long term: RTX (193.92) is 'Buy zone, wait for the chart' because sellers lead on volume (up/down 0.74); Tuesday's report can fix that or break the zone, so do not sell a put through it. ISRG (426.70) is 'Accumulate on pullback': correction to Sunday's brief, it sits inside its 342.70 to 463.65 zone, not above it; the rating is about the price being 8.9% above its 50 day average. A post report drop toward the 50 day (391.67) is the setup to wait for. CLF (12.12) is rated Avoid: no trade on a beat. JPM (339.72) is 'Buy zone now'; let tonight's bank reports pass first.

cycle.big_cycle: Four of five forces are active. External order shifted: Washington waived new Russia tariffs to get diesel flowing before the midterms, while Hormuz stays shut. Internal order: riots in France and fuel prices before the Nov 3 US vote. Debt and money: AI lenders pulling back. Technology: Meta, Tesla and Lam this week test who pays for AI.

history.when: October 2008, the chip index's eight day slide
history.what: The Philadelphia chip index fell eight days in a row in October 2008, the record this year's streak just matched (Reuters). Then the trigger was a credit freeze that cut orders across the economy.
history.lesson: Long chip streaks tend to come when credit is breaking, not when demand is. The bounce came only after lenders stopped pulling back.

cycle.differences: October 2008 replaces the 1990 recession example today because the new fact is credit stress in AI lending lining up with the chip slide. What is different: in 2008 demand for chips was collapsing; today TSMC just raised its 2026 growth to about 44% (Oct 15), so the stress is in who finances the build, not in whether buyers want chips. That makes it narrower, but lenders can still slow the build.

principle.text: Truth, or more precisely an accurate understanding of reality, is the essential foundation for any good outcome.
principle.applied: A green premarket feels like the selloff is over. The reality is that lenders are still marking down AI debt. Act on closes and volume, not on hope.
